From myth to marketplace: designing avatars for good
abstract: The market for digital avatars is expanding rapidly, yet consumer adoption and experiences with the technology remain uneven, highlighting the need to understand the psychological, social, and ethical effects of avatars. Building on interdisciplinary theory, we propose a conceptual model of ethical avatar design for consumer wellbeing, centred on self-congruence and humanisation, and moderated by realism and skills. The model integrates insights from the Proteus Effect, Computers-Are-Social-Actors framework, and Social Comparison Theory, and is operationalised through a self–avatar continuum that classifies forms of customisation. While avatars enable engagement, self-expression, and perspective-taking, they may also amplify risks such as stereotype reinforcement, Uncanny Valley effects, or idealized body standards. The framework presented here provides actionable strategies for designing avatars that align with user values, foster wellbeing, and encourage prosocial behaviour, offering both managerial guidance and directions for future research in marketing, health, and immersive digital environments.

title: Measuring corporate political identity and its impact on tax compliance behaviour: evidence from China
Why are peer-to-peer ratings almost always positive? How market contextual factors can systematically affect consumer motivations for eWOM
abstract: Sharing economy consumers rely on ratings and reviews as a source of trust. But peer-to-peer ratings are overwhelmingly positive, which can limit their informational value and erode trust. We use a mixed-method approach to investigate whether and why peer-to-peer ratings are more positive than ratings for comparable commercial services, including a large-scale analysis of Airbnb listings, as well as preregistered surveys and experiments. We find that peer-to-peer consumers both inflate the ratings they provide and selectively withhold low ratings through two motivational pathways: a promotion-focused motivation to help non-professional providers and a prevention-focused motivation for self-protection from retaliation, respectively. We show how the peer-to-peer context systematically shifts consumers toward these motivations, identifying self-protection as a distinct, avoidance-based motive that contrasts with traditional gain-focused eWOM motivations. Finally, we identify platform interventions to reduce rating positivity by attenuating self-protection concerns and redirecting consumers’ desire to help providers toward alternative forms of support.

title: Exploring the impact of virtual reality on voluntourism engagement and well-being
abstract: Immersive technologies are increasingly used in promotional contexts. However, their potential to foster prosocial behaviors remains underexplored. This study examines how virtual reality (VR) shapes willingness to engage in voluntourism and how this willingness relates to psychological well-being. Across four studies using netnography, experiment, focus group, and structural modeling, we develop and test an integrative framework grounded in self-determination and self-congruence theories. Study 1 identifies perceived (in)authenticity and curiosity as key motivational pathways. Study 2 demonstrates that VR increases willingness to engage indirectly through these mechanisms and that the authenticity pathway weakens among individuals higher in cultural adventurousness and aspiring indulger orientation. Studies 3 and 4 reveal that self-congruence positively predicts willingness to engage, whereas moral obligation is negatively associated with it. Finally, willingness to engage positively relates to psychological well-being. These findings extend research on immersive technology and voluntourism by showing how VR-based appeals can strengthen prosocial engagement.

title: How virtual reality shapes visitor experiences during the pre-visit stage: The role of perceived realism
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) may enhance the pre-visit phase of the visitor journey by allowing would-be tourists to preview destinations and promoting the value of their experience and their well-being. The realism of VR experiences plays a key role at this stage, yet current research reveals mixed findings. Grounded in the stimulus–organism–response model, this study investigates how VR content with different levels of realism influences affective responses and, in turn, shapes visitor intentions and behaviors during the pre-visit phase. A laboratory experiment using a multimethod approach combining self-reported, neurophysiological, and behavioral measures revealed that VR experiences elicit psychophysiological activation closely associated with affective responses, highlighting the potential of immersive technologies to enhance the pre-visit experience. Furthermore, although high realism enhances perceived authenticity, less realistic VR environments are more effective in stimulating travel intentions and engagement with the tourist place. Practical insights are offered for businesses in the tourism sector.

Just energy transition, market making and the missed affordances of cleantech
abstract: A just transition entails decarbonization that is equitable across the energy lifecycle, integrating economic, social, and ecological justice. While its importance is widely recognized and efforts to operationalize it are growing, clean technology-enabled transitions often fall short of these ambitions. Emerging scholarship proposes non-negotiable minimum boundaries to evaluate whether transitions are genuinely “just.” Yet, the processes through which such boundaries are shaped remain underexplored. This paper develops theory on how intermediary-led market-making processes shape transition boundaries. We show that intermediaries’ efforts to broker the diverse affordances of clean technologies may restrict or expand the range of technological affordances realized in socio-technical transitions, leading to transition pathways that may be more or less just. We contribute to the literature on socio-technical transition by theorizing how the unobtrusive power of market intermediaries shapes transition processes. These insights invite further research into how intermediary practices can be reimagined to realize just transitions.

How leaders build employee trust in artificial intelligence: voice opportunities, humility, and trust transfer
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly central to organizational work, yet employee trust in AI remains fragile. Although prior research has primarily explained trust in AI through technological characteristics such as transparency, reliability, and accuracy, we argue that trust in AI is also shaped by the social context in which employees encounter these systems. Drawing on affect-as-information theory and social information processing theory, we develop and test a model in which leader-provided voice opportunities reduce employees’ negative affect about AI-related work experiences, thereby enhancing perceptions of leader trustworthiness and, in turn, trust in AI. We further propose that this indirect effect depends on leader humility, because humility signals that employee concerns will be received in a respectful, open, and non-defensive manner. Results from a multi-wave field survey and an experiment support this model.

title: Dynamic Capabilities May Not Be Efficient: A Multiyear Econometric Analysis of Multiple Performance Dimensions Shows the Robust Absence of Systematic Relationships
abstract: Although dynamic capabilities (DCs) theoretically constitute the evolution of a firm’s capabilities, the research tends to examine this phenomenon from a static perspective. This paper presents a methodology for capturing dynamic capabilities to understand their longitudinal effect. An analysis of an eleven-year dynamic panel dataset reveals that the effects of dynamic capabilities on several different performance dimensions are predominantly null. The results show that sensing, seizing, and reconfiguration capabilities do not lead universally to superior outcomes, including technological intensity and environmental dynamism, and do not alter the firm’s situation. Notably, null effects were observed for both the general model and when firms were grouped according to different levels of technology intensity. These insights advance DC theory by highlighting the conditional and sometimes contradictory nature of capability‒performance relationships, offering practical guidance for managers navigating strategic investments in dynamic environments.

title: Are aspects of ESG created equal? Examining B2B firms’ ESG content on social media

The impact of blockchain technology on supply chain trust formation and development: The case of the pharmaceutical network
abstract: This study explores the role of blockchain technology’s (BCT) in trust formation and development within the U.S. pharmaceutical supply chain (PSC), using the MediLedger network as a case study. Grounded in socio-technical systems (STS) theory, we develop a conceptual model, which serves as the analytical framework to examine how supply chain trust evolves within a BCT-based ecosystem. We triangulate data from seven in-depth elite interviews with senior executives, alongside secondary data from company reports, case studies and white papers. The findings indicate that BCT significantly influences trust within the PSC, particularly by redistributing and reconfiguring trust across socio-technical boundaries and fostering a new dimension of trust: trust in network. This is facilitated through BCT-enabled mechanisms that accelerate trust formation processes, which is particularly important in the contingent PSC environment. Finally, we propose a BCT-based hierarchical supply chain trust framework that articulates and conceptualises the different mechanisms and dimensions of trust.

title: Reality or fantasy? How human and virtual influencers can more effectively narrate brand stories
Robotic pets as resources: transforming the lives of the unseen and overlooked
abstract: Older people often feel “invisible” in society, experiencing vulnerability due to restricted resources and diminished control. Their loved ones may also experience a spillover of this vulnerability. This study investigates robotic pets (robopets) as artificial intelligence–enabled resources that can enhance well-being for both groups. Automated text analysis of online customer reviews across four reviewer segments reveals that robopets’ visual and tactile features enhance their perceived realism. This realism, alongside beneficiary attachment and prior pet ownership, positively relates to online ratings and beneficiary well-being. Qualitative analysis shows that robopets reduce vulnerability by restoring beneficiaries’ capacity to care for something while helping loved ones manage difficult emotions. Studying lived experiences of robopet ownership transcends the typically temporary consumer–robopet interactions depicted in prior research. Our findings inform the design and marketing of robopets to those experiencing vulnerability. Ultimately, we provide evidence that robopets can enhance quality of life for older “invisibles” and those who care for them.

On the right side of nature: indigenous spatialities, justice, and the reconfiguration of environmental governance
abstract: This article examines how Indigenous spatialities reconstitute environmental governance systems historically shaped by colonialism. It draws on the Rights of Nature (RoN) concept, focusing on the legal recognition of the Whanganui River under Aotearoa New Zealand’s Te Awa Tupua Act . Based on qualitative analysis of legal texts, interviews, news articles, and governance documents, the study identifies three spatial dynamics: unfixing cartographies, drawing decision-making inward, and circulating authority laterally. These dynamics respectively disrupt colonial territorial representations, recentre decision-making processes toward the river, and redistribute authority across relational governance networks. Building on these findings, I argue that Indigenous spatialities enable ontological coexistence within environmental governance, allowing Indigenous and Western understandings of nature to be negotiated within the same governance framework without requiring one to fully subsume the other. The analysis further demonstrates how, through Indigenous spatialities, more-than-human agency emerges as a central mechanism of governance transformation, with important implications for energy justice.

title: Unpacking the role of identity in family business succession: A systematic literature review and integrative framework
abstract: Identity has emerged as a prominent lens in family business research, particularly in understanding the psychological, relational, and organisational complexities of intergenerational succession. Despite its growing importance, research on identity in family business succession remains conceptually fragmented and theoretically inconsistent. Drawing on a systematic literature review, we develop an integrative framework that clarifies how identity shapes succession processes and outcomes. By taking an identity perspective, we synthesise motives, processes, contents, and outcomes across individual, relational, and collective levels, and reconceptualise succession as a multilevel process of identity evolution. By positioning identity as the central mechanism through which families make sense of continuity and change, we offer a unified lens that connects psychological and organisational perspectives to explain how families sustain who they are across generations. The proposed framework delineates the structural contours of the field, defines core constructs and their interrelationships, and outlines a forward-looking research agenda for future research.
